newsitem.title: USA: AIDS studies measure drug effectiveness in babies.
newsitem.headline: AIDS studies measure drug effectiveness in babies.

text.p: A new study has confirmed something about babies that doctors already knew about adults: the more HIV there is in the blood, the faster the deadly immunity disease AIDS appears.

In tests on 106 newborns infected with HIV, a research team led by Dr. William Shearer of the Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, found that babies with the highest levels of HIV were at a greater risk of quickly developing one of the immunity-related diseases that are the hallmarks of AIDS.
Their finding, published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, raised the possibility that early treatment with new anti-HIV drugs may slow or prevent the development of AIDS in infants.
The Shearer study involved children born at hospitals in Boston, Chicago, New York City, Houston, San Juan, Puerto Rico and Worcester, Mass., between 1990 and 1993.

The study was conducted before tests found that treating a pregnant HIV-infected woman with AZT could help prevent AIDS from being spread to her fetus. Only about 1-in-5 of the pregnant women in the study received AZT before their children were born.

The Shearer group also concluded that the amount of HIV in the blood usually started at a low level immediately after birth and increased rapidly. The levels then gradually declined during the first two years of life.

That pattern may be significant. Shearer and his colleagues said the fact that HIV levels were low after birth suggested most newborns either "have acquired their infection very close to the time of birth" or there was some undiscovered protective factor that hindered the growth of new HIV particles until after the child was born.
A separate study also published in Thursday's edition, concluded that a combination of three drugs could reduce the amount of HIV in the blood of newborns without causing serious side effects.
However, the effectiveness of the three-drug treatment was not compared with conventional therapy and the treatments only lasted for six months, which meant further testing was needed.

The three drugs were nevirapine, sold under the brand name Viramune by Boehringer-Ingelheim; didanosine, made by Bristol-Myers Squibb under the brand name Videx; and AZT, also known as Retrovir, made by Glaxo Wellcome.
In a test of eight infants and children with HIV, the researchers found that seven of them had significant reductions in the amount of virus in the blood during the six months of treatment.
For two of the children, the HIV virus seemed to disappear completely, but it reappeared in one of the two.

The research team, led by Dr. Katherine Luzuriaga of the University of Massachusetts Medical School in Worcester, said the likelihood that drugs could eradicate the AIDS virus in a child might depend on whether a drug could get into the central nervous system or other areas of the body where the virus tended to seek sanctuary.
